title: Japanese Artist ARKO’s Rice-Straw Sculptures Revive Traditional Craft
summary: Her intricate, hand-stitched creations elevate a humble natural material.
body_markdown:
[Breath of Layers rice-straw wall sculpture, 2025, by ARKO](https://www.1stdibs.com/furniture/wall-decorations/decorative-art/arko-rice-straw-art-wall-12-sculpture-contemporary-art-japanese-craft-japandi/id-f_50142232/)


Tokyo is the third-most populated city on earth, a place where time never stands still and the urban landscape positively pulsates with neon shop signs, immersive 3D billboards and a seemingly endless procession of people. It is also a city of striking contradictions, where futuristic architecture and dazzling commercial districts sit alongside centuries-old shrines, traditional-craft boutiques and lantern-lit *izakayas* (casual bar-restaurants) tucked away on narrow backstreets.


This counterpoint of flux and movement with peace and quiet is expressed in the work of Tokyo-based artist[ARKO](https://www.1stdibs.com/creators/arko/furniture/) , who transforms a humble natural material, rice straw, into layered compositions characterized by golden hues and undulating forms. At once organic and totemic, her intricate straw wall hangings command attention, emanating warmth, order and a mesmeric tranquility. This quality has everything to do with her artistic process: Individual straw stems, or culms, are carefully teased away from their cluster and hand-stitched together, their ends meticulously trimmed to create intricate patterns and beautifully uniform lines.


Individual pieces of straw are hand-stitched together to form the[sculpture](https://www.1stdibs.com/furniture/wall-decorations/decorative-art/arko-rice-straw-art-wall-12-sculpture-contemporary-art-japanese-craft-japandi/id-f_50142232/) .


This process, which can take months to complete, mirrors the intricate handwork of haute couture, with ARKO shaping the straw into rich tapestry-like compositions, sometimes rectangular, sometimes circular, as in this piece, aptly named *[Breath of Layers](https://www.1stdibs.com/furniture/wall-decorations/decorative-art/arko-rice-straw-art-wall-12-sculpture-contemporary-art-japanese-craft-japandi/id-f_50142232/)* . Here, a spiraling central nucleus of red thread gives way to a series of lively fringed layers that radiate outwards, creating a compelling sense of movement and vitality, as though the work were a living entity.


Central to ARKO’s work is the reinterpretation of tradition through a modern lens. Rice straw was once integral to everyday Japanese life, employed in a wide range of household objects, from floor mats and seating to *waraji* sandals and futon filling.


Its use is now much more limited, with straw artistry mainly applied to braided *shimekazari* wreaths, sacred New Year decorations traditionally hung to invite good fortune into the home. In ARKO’s hands, the ancient, resilient material is liberated from its traditional utilitarian and symbolic functions to reveal its inherent beauty.


“What particularly distinguishes this piece — even among her other works — is its complex layering and a certain wild, untamed quality,” says Naoki Sato, of[Somewhere Tokyo](https://www.1stdibs.com/dealers/somewhere-tokyo/) gallery, which offers ARKO’s work on 1stDibs.


“For the Japanese people, straw is something deeply familiar, yet it has now become something that feels distant precisely because science and technology have advanced so far,” says Naoki Sato, founder and owner of[Somewhere Tokyo](https://www.1stdibs.com/dealers/somewhere-tokyo/) , which is offering *Breath of Layers* on 1stDibs. “I believe it is necessary to reflect on the fundamental elements of nature. ARKO’s works serve as objects that prompt such reflection, even amidst the context of urban life.”


In his bijou gallery on the outskirts of Shibuya, one of Tokyo’s busiest commercial districts, Sato displays *Breath of Layers* alongside two other large-scale works by ARKO. Softly shimmering in the gallery’s warm glow, the three pieces seem like portals into an alternative universe. Their intricately arranged, finely trimmed segments fan out in striking starburst formations, creating an hypnotic effect and offering a momentary escape from the frenetic energy of the city.


For Sato, *Breath of Layers* possesses a special presence, expressing something profound about our relationship with the natural world. “What particularly distinguishes this piece — even among her other works — is its complex layering and a certain wild, untamed quality,” the gallerist explains. “It features a striking contrast, blending moments of stillness with elements of dynamic movement. It might be an overstatement, but I feel that modern society has become so technologically advanced that it has drifted far away from the natural environment and the ecosystems that surround us. To me, her work seems to capture the inherent, multifaceted nature of our world, the complex, interwoven tapestry of living things and the natural realm. I believe these works, so vibrant with a sense of life, can at times serve to remind us of our own original, primordial state.”
